meta.title: How Deep Should Mulch Be? Two to Three Inches | HD Landscape
meta.description: Two to three inches in a bed, kept off the trunk. Why mulch volcanoes can kill trees, how to fix one, and the depths MSU Extension and Penn State recommend.

title: How deep mulch should be, and why **volcanoes can kill trees.**
lede: Mulch should be two to three inches deep and kept off the trunk. More is not better. Mulch piled against a tree looks tidy and does real damage where you cannot see it, and it is easy to fix once you know what to look for.
short: Two to three inches is the right depth for most beds. Michigan State University Extension says that is adequate and that more is not better.
If a bed already has mulch in it, about an inch is enough to freshen it.
Keep mulch off the trunk. MSU's rule is a six inch bare ring at the base of the tree: a doughnut, not a volcano.
A mulch volcano keeps bark wet, cuts off oxygen to the roots and invites rot, insects and rodents.
A volcano can be fixed. Pull the mulch back until you can see where the trunk flares out.

sections.h: Two to three inches, with a few exceptions
p: Most landscape beds need two to three inches of mulch. That is MSU Extension's number, and it says plainly that more is not better. Penn State, University of Illinois and University of Minnesota extension all say 2 to 4 inches, and other MSU guidance allows 3 to 4 inches, including in a brand new bed. None of them aim past 4. Two to three inches is the number to plan on.

sections.h: Check what is already in the bed
p: Most beds do not need a full new layer every spring. Penn State Extension says adding new mulch over old each year has the same effect as laying it too deep all at once.

Dig down with a hand trowel until you hit soil, then measure. If you already have two to three inches, an inch is plenty. If you have more than that, some of the old mulch needs to come out before anything new goes down. Break up matted layers with a rake so water can get through.
A depth check belongs at the start of any [mulching job](/mulching/). Mulch spreading is what our Google reviews bring up most, and what sits under the top layer is the part you never see.

sections.h: A mulch volcano is a cone of mulch against the trunk
p: Penn State Extension says the practice is never recommended and should not be used. University of Illinois Extension calls it a harmful practice that spells death for the tree.
It looks neat, which is why it keeps showing up. The trouble is underneath.

sections.h: Why a volcano can kill a tree
p: A mulch volcano holds water against the bark and keeps air from the roots. From there, six things can go wrong.
list: **Wet bark.** Bark that stays wet can rot. Penn State says constantly wet bark can kill the living inner bark, and Illinois says rot can reach the tissue that moves water through the tree.
**Less oxygen.** Thick mulch and waterlogged soil keep oxygen from reaching the roots, which can kill them. Heavy clay already drains slowly, so there is less room for error.
**Disease.** MSU calls that dark, moist pile an invitation for root rot. Penn State says wet, decaying bark lets disease in, and the result can be fungal cankers and root rots.
**Insects.** Penn State says moist mulch against the trunk attracts carpenter ants and termites.
**Rodents.** Illinois says mulch against the trunk invites mice and voles that chew bark. On a young tree, Penn State says that can girdle the stem.
**Heat.** Penn State notes that thick, wet mulch can heat up as high as 140 degrees.

sections.h: Mulch in a doughnut, not a cone
p: Think of a doughnut, with the tree in the hole. Keep about six inches of bare ground around the trunk, then let the mulch come up to full depth as it moves out.
You should be able to see the root flare, the spot where the trunk widens as it meets the soil. If the trunk goes straight into the mulch like a telephone pole, it is buried.

Extension numbers for that gap vary. Illinois says two inches, and Penn State says 3 to 5 inches on young trees and 8 to 10 on mature ones. MSU's six inches sits in the middle and is an easy one to remember.

Wide beats deep. Penn State's line is to mulch wide, not deep, ideally out to the drip line at the edge of the canopy. MSU makes the same point from the other side: tree and shrub roots spread well out from the trunk, so a small circle at the base mostly just keeps mowers and trimmers off the bark.

sections.h: How to fix a mulch volcano
p: These are Penn State Extension's steps, and you can do them with a hand trowel.
list: Dig in by hand to see how deep the mulch really is.
Pull it back from the trunk until the root flare is showing.
Spread the extra out toward the drip line, keeping the layer at 4 inches or less.
Stop if you reach soil and still see no flare. Some trees are planted too deep, and Penn State says to talk to an arborist before digging around a buried flare.
after: If you would rather not do it yourself, point it out when Jake walks the property, and the fix can go on your estimate. For work on the tree itself, we handle [tree trimming and smaller removals](/tree-trimming-and-removal/). The big ones we hand off to a tree company.

sections.h: Shrubs and perennials need room too
p: The same rule works at a smaller scale. Keep mulch back from shrub stems, and go easy around perennials, because a deep layer can smother them. [Weeds come out](/weeding/) before the mulch goes down, because MSU says mulch smothers annual and some perennial weeds, not all of them.
Thinking about stone instead? We compare them in [mulch or stone for a Michigan bed](/journal/mulch-or-stone/).
